# Communicating visually
## Visual communication
Visual arts is about making and understanding meaning through images and objects. The formal elements are line, shape, form, colour, tone, texture and space. The principles of design are how the elements are arranged: balance, contrast, emphasis, rhythm, movement, unity and proportion. Composition is the arrangement of elements within an artwork.

## Analysing art
Formal analysis looks at how an artwork is made and how its elements create effects. Contextual analysis looks at the time, place and culture in which it was made. Interpretation is a reasoned reading of what an artwork means. Use subject-specific vocabulary to describe media, techniques and processes.

## Key terms
Formal elements: line, shape, form, colour, tone, texture and space
Composition: the arrangement of elements in an artwork
Contrast: the difference between elements, such as light and dark
Formal analysis: analysing how an artwork is made
Contextual analysis: analysing the context in which an artwork was made
Lenses: identities and relationships:
# Lenses: identities and relationships
## The lens
Identities and relationships is a lens for exploring art. It asks how artists explore who they are, how they relate to others and how identity is represented. Themes include self-portraiture, family, gender, cultural identity, community and belonging.

## Examples
Frida Kahlo's self-portraits explore identity, pain and Mexican heritage. Kehinde Wiley's portraits place Black subjects in poses from European art history. Representation is how people and ideas are shown in art. Identity is how people see themselves and are seen by others.

## Key terms
Lens: a way of looking at art through a theme
Self-portrait: an artwork that depicts the artist
Representation: how people and ideas are shown in art
Identity: how people see themselves and are seen by others
Lenses: environments:
# Lenses: environments
## The lens
Environments is a lens for exploring art. It asks how artists respond to natural, built and imagined environments, and to issues such as climate change and urbanization. Themes include landscape, cities, interiors, ecology and place.

## Examples
Land art uses the landscape as material, as in Robert Smithson's Spiral Jetty. Site-specific art is made for a particular location. Olafur Eliasson's installations explore climate and perception. An installation is an artwork that transforms a space.

## Key terms
Land art: art made in and from the landscape
Site-specific art: art made for a particular location
Installation: an artwork that transforms a space
Landscape: an artwork depicting natural scenery
Lenses: past, present and future:
# Lenses: past, present and future
## The lens
Past, present and future is a lens for exploring art. It asks how artists respond to history and tradition, comment on the present and imagine the future. Themes include memory, heritage, appropriation, innovation and speculative futures.

## Examples
Appropriation is borrowing existing images or objects to create new meaning, as in Andy Warhol's work. Artists may reinterpret traditional techniques with new media. Digital art uses technology such as code, video and virtual reality. A movement is a style or tendency in art shared by a group of artists in a period, such as Cubism or Surrealism.

## Key terms
Appropriation: borrowing existing images to create new meaning
Art movement: a style shared by artists in a period
Digital art: art made with digital technology
Heritage: traditions and art inherited from the past
Art-making inquiries portfolio:
# Art-making inquiries portfolio
## The portfolio
The art-making inquiries portfolio documents your exploration of ideas, materials and techniques over the course. It shows experimentation, research, reflection and development of ideas.

## Doing it well
Investigate a range of media and processes. Experimentation is testing materials and techniques to find out what they can do. Record your process with annotated images. Reflection is thinking critically about what worked and why. Link your inquiries to artists and contexts you have studied, and show how your ideas develop.

## Key terms
Experimentation: testing materials and techniques
Reflection: thinking critically about your work
Annotation: notes explaining your process
Art-making inquiry: an investigation through making art
Connections study:
# Connections study
## The connections study
The connections study is a critical investigation of artworks by different artists, linked to your own art-making. It analyses and compares artworks from different contexts.

## Doing it well
Choose artworks that connect in a meaningful way, such as theme, technique or purpose. Analyse each with formal and contextual analysis. Compare and contrast them, and explain how they influenced your own work. Cite your sources accurately.

## Key terms
Connections study: a critical investigation linking artworks to your own
Compare and contrast: show similarities and differences
Citation: a reference to a source
Influence: how one artwork or artist shapes another
Resolved artworks:
# Resolved artworks
## Resolved artworks
A resolved artwork is a finished piece that fully realizes your intentions. Resolved artworks show technical skill, purposeful use of media and a clear concept. An artist's intention is what they aim to communicate.

## Developing a body of work
A body of work is a coherent collection of artworks connected by ideas or processes. Develop your work through experimentation and refinement, and make deliberate choices about scale, media and presentation.

## Key terms
Resolved artwork: a finished artwork that fully realizes intentions
Intention: what the artist aims to communicate
Body of work: a coherent collection of connected artworks
Refinement: improving a work through development
Selected resolved artworks and exhibitio:
# Selected resolved artworks and exhibition text
## The exhibition
For assessment, you select resolved artworks and present them with an exhibition text. Curation is the selection and arrangement of artworks for display. An exhibition text explains your intentions and the connections between your artworks.

## Doing it well
Select works that together show your strongest ideas and skills. Consider how the arrangement and lighting affect the viewer. Write a clear, concise exhibition text that explains your concepts without describing every detail. Each artwork needs a title, medium and size.

## Key terms
Curation: selecting and arranging artworks for display
Exhibition text: a written explanation of your exhibited work
Medium: the material used to make an artwork
Viewer: the person experiencing the artwork
